## In 60 seconds

Couple excitable cells through conductances and the action potential travels. Below threshold, a fiber is a leaky
**cable**: a held voltage decays over a **length constant** set by membrane and axial resistances. Above threshold,
each depolarized region pulls its neighbor past threshold and a wave moves at a steady **conduction velocity**. The
**bidomain** model keeps the intracellular and extracellular spaces separate; when both are equally anisotropic it
collapses to the simpler **monodomain** model, which is what most simulations use. Velocity scales with the square
root of conductivity, and because cardiac fibers conduct better along their length, waves from a point spread as
ellipses. Curved fronts are slower than flat ones, and a source too small to excite the tissue around it fails.
Mapping systems measure the outcome of all of this, and what they show depends on the direction they measure in.

## From the field

- **Fibers make velocity directional.** Canine epicardial excitation spread 2.4 times faster along fibers than across
  them [@roberts1979]; in calf trabeculae the ratio was 3.0 [@clerc1976]. A velocity measured along a line that is
  not aligned with the fibers lies in between (demo m09-d2).
- **Low-voltage tissue conducts slowly.** In persistent atrial fibrillation patients, left atrial velocity averaged
  1.0 m/s in normal-voltage areas of the anterior wall and 0.6 m/s in low-voltage areas [@heil2023].
- **Monodomain is usually enough.** In organ-scale models of the human heart, propagation was only 2% faster in the
  bidomain model than in the monodomain model, and electrograms were visually indistinguishable when no current was
  applied [@potse2006].
- **Curvature matters at small scales.** Wavefront curvature governs propagation from small electrodes, out of narrow
  structures and around sharp obstacles [@fast1997]; it is one reason a stimulus can capture in one place and not in
  another.

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $V$ transmembrane voltage; $\varphi_e$ extracellular potential; $r_m$ membrane resistance
times length, $r_i$, $r_e$ intracellular and extracellular axial resistances per length, $c_m$ membrane capacitance
per length; $\lambda$ length constant (mm), $\tau_m$ membrane time constant (ms). $\sigma_i$, $\sigma_e$ conductivity
tensors, $\sigma_m$ monodomain conductivity; $\chi$ membrane area per volume; $C_m$ capacitance per area; $I_{\text{ion}}$
ionic current per area; $D = \sigma_m/(\chi C_m)$ diffusion coefficient (mm²/ms). CV conduction velocity (mm/ms = m/s);
subscripts L and T along and across fibers; $\theta$ angle to the fibers; $\kappa$ front curvature (1/mm), $c_0$ plane
wave velocity.

### The passive cable

A fiber with leaky membrane and axial resistance obeys the cable equation:

$$
\lambda^2\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} = \tau_m\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + V, \qquad \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{r_m}{r_i + r_e}}, \quad \tau_m = r_m c_m
$$ {#eq-m09-cable}

Hold one end at $V_0$ and the steady state is $V_0e^{-x/\lambda}$: 37% of the voltage remains one length constant away.
The cable equation is the subthreshold part of propagation; it says how far a depolarized region can pull its
neighbors toward threshold.

**Key takeaways**

- Subthreshold voltage spreads over a length constant $\sqrt{r_m/(r_i + r_e)}$.
- Lower axial resistance means a longer reach.

### Bidomain and monodomain

Tissue is two interpenetrating conductors, the cells and the space around them, coupled through the membrane. Current
conservation in each gives the bidomain equations:

$$
\nabla\cdot\big(\sigma_i\nabla(V + \varphi_e)\big) = \chi\Big(C_m\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + I_{\text{ion}}\Big), \qquad \nabla\cdot\big((\sigma_i + \sigma_e)\nabla\varphi_e\big) = -\nabla\cdot(\sigma_i\nabla V)
$$ {#eq-m09-bidomain}

In 1D, with no net current along the fiber, the second equation gives
$\varphi_e = -\sigma_iV/(\sigma_i + \sigma_e)$ plus a constant. Substituting into the first leaves one equation for
$V$:

$$
\chi\Big(C_m\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + I_{\text{ion}}\Big) = \nabla\cdot(\sigma_m\nabla V), \qquad \sigma_m = \sigma_i(\sigma_i + \sigma_e)^{-1}\sigma_e
$$ {#eq-m09-monodomain}

The same reduction holds in 2D and 3D when $\sigma_e$ is a multiple of $\sigma_i$, that is, when both domains have the
same anisotropy ratio. They do not: from Clerc's resistance ratios in calf trabeculae, the intracellular domain is 9.4
times more conductive along fibers than across them, the extracellular domain 2.7 times [@clerc1976]. Even so,
organ-scale comparisons find the monodomain model accurate for propagation without applied currents [@potse2006].
Stimulation and defibrillation, where current is injected, need the bidomain model.

**Key takeaways**

- The bidomain model has two potentials; the monodomain model has one, with conductivity $\sigma_i\sigma_e/(\sigma_i + \sigma_e)$.
- The reduction is exact in 1D and for equal anisotropy ratios, and a good approximation for propagation in general.

### Conduction velocity

Divide the monodomain equation by $\chi C_m$: conductivity appears only through $D = \sigma_m/(\chi C_m)$. Stretching
all lengths by $\sqrt k$ turns $D$ into $kD$ and leaves the equation otherwise unchanged, so:

$$
\text{CV} \propto \sqrt{D}, \qquad \frac{\text{CV}_L}{\text{CV}_T} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{m,L}}{\sigma_{m,T}}}
$$ {#eq-m09-cv}

m33 uses the same scaling to tune conductivities
([eq-m33-cv-scaling](m33-capstone-digital-twin.qmd#eq-m33-cv-scaling)). On a Mitchell–Schaeffer cable, quadrupling
$D$ doubles the velocity to within 0.2%, and $D$ = 0.86 mm²/ms gives 1.0 m/s (lab part B). Clerc's resistance ratios
give monodomain conductivities whose square-root ratio is 2.82, against a measured velocity ratio of 3.0
[@clerc1976]. Velocity also depends on the grid: a 0.4-mm grid computes a wave 2.7% slower than a 0.05-mm grid.

::: {.demo #m09-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m09-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m09-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m09-d1-cable-velocity.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: a 20-mm Mitchell–Schaeffer cable (@eq-m09-monodomain) by forward Euler, steps of 0.005 ms or less, no-flux
  ends, stimulus on the first 0.5 mm for 1 ms; velocity from a fit over the middle third. Tested against
  `epml.propagation`.
- Parameters: membrane constants as in m08 [@nietoramos2023]; $D$ and the grid spacing are free choices for
  illustration.
- What it ignores: discrete cells and gap junctions, fiber structure, curvature and the extracellular space.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Velocity scales as the square root of conductivity; anisotropy in velocity is the square root of anisotropy in
  conductivity.
- Coarse grids slow simulated waves; check convergence before trusting a simulated velocity.

### Anisotropy

With fibers along one axis, a wave from a point eventually travels at $\text{CV}_L$ along and $\text{CV}_T$ across
them, so its far-field isochrones are ellipses:

$$
T(\mathbf x) = \sqrt{\frac{x_L^2}{\text{CV}_L^2} + \frac{x_T^2}{\text{CV}_T^2}}, \qquad c(\theta) = \frac{\text{CV}_L\,\text{CV}_T}{\sqrt{\text{CV}_T^2\cos^2\theta + \text{CV}_L^2\sin^2\theta}}
$$ {#eq-m09-anisotropy}

$c(\theta)$ is the apparent speed along a ray at angle $\theta$ to the fibers. With a ratio of 3 and 1.0 m/s along
fibers, a mapping line at 30° to them sees 0.58 m/s and one at 60° sees 0.38 m/s. In a simulated sheet with
$D_T = D_L/9$, the measured velocity ratio rises from 2.85 to 2.99 between 5 and 19 mm from the stimulus as the front
flattens (lab part D).

::: {.demo #m09-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m09-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m09-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m09-d2-anisotropy.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m09-anisotropy in uniform tissue, isochrones every 5 ms; the readout is $c(\theta)$ for the horizontal
  line. Tested against `epml.propagation`.
- Parameters: 1.0 m/s along fibers, reported for normal-voltage left atrium [@heil2023]; the velocity ratio (default 3.0
  [@clerc1976]) and the fiber angle are adjustable.
- What it ignores: curvature near the stimulus (part D of the lab), fiber rotation through the wall, boundaries and
  heterogeneity.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Point stimuli give elliptical isochrones elongated along the fibers.
- A velocity measured along an arbitrary line depends on its angle to the fibers.

### Curvature

An expanding front feeds more tissue ahead of it than a flat one, so it slows:

$$
c(\kappa) \approx c_0 - D\,\kappa
$$ {#eq-m09-curvature}

For a circle of radius $r$, $\kappa = 1/r$. In a radially symmetric Mitchell–Schaeffer simulation with
$D$ = 0.1 mm²/ms the front speed matches $c_0 - D/r$ within 2% from 3 mm outward (lab part E). Shrink the stimulated
disk and the wave eventually fails: it launched from a 0.5-mm disk and failed from 0.3 mm, the same order as
$D/c_0$ = 0.29 mm. Curvature and this source–sink balance shape propagation from electrodes, out of narrow channels and
around obstacles [@fast1997; @kleber2004].

**Key takeaways**

- Convex fronts are slower by about $D\kappa$.
- A source must excite a large enough region to overcome the sink around it.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Velocity maps (m25) summarize propagation, and reported values differ with tissue
state: 1.0 m/s in normal-voltage and 0.6 m/s in low-voltage left atrial areas in one study of persistent atrial
fibrillation [@heil2023]. Velocity also depends on direction: experimental velocity ratios along and across fibers of
2.4 and 3.0 [@roberts1979; @clerc1976] mean that a value measured along an arbitrary line mixes tissue properties with
geometry. Slowing and block at curved fronts and narrow structures [@fast1997; @kleber2004] are the substrate for the
reentry mechanisms of m10.

**What the evidence is.** Experimental measurements in animal tissue [@clerc1976; @roberts1979], a clinical mapping
study [@heil2023], a modelling comparison [@potse2006] and reviews [@fast1997; @kleber2004].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **In which direction was velocity measured, relative to the fibers?** (@eq-m09-anisotropy)
- **How close to the pacing site?** Near the source, curvature slows the front (@eq-m09-curvature).
- **For simulated velocities: what grid, and was convergence checked?** (@eq-m09-cv)

## How experts think

Before trusting a conduction velocity, ask:

1. **Along which direction?** Compare it with the fibers (@eq-m09-anisotropy).
2. **How far from the source?** Near the pacing site the front is curved and slower (@eq-m09-curvature).
3. **Plane wave or not?** Velocity formulas assume a locally flat front.
4. **For a model: monodomain or bidomain, and why?** Applied currents need the bidomain (@eq-m09-bidomain).
5. **For a simulation: grid converged?** (@eq-m09-cv)

One sentence to keep: **velocity is a property of the wave as much as of the tissue.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Cable (@eq-m09-cable) | $\lambda = \sqrt{r_m/(r_i + r_e)}$; steady decay $e^{-x/\lambda}$ |
| Bidomain (@eq-m09-bidomain) | two potentials, two conductivity tensors |
| Monodomain (@eq-m09-monodomain) | $\sigma_m = \sigma_i(\sigma_i + \sigma_e)^{-1}\sigma_e$; exact in 1D or for equal anisotropy ratios |
| Velocity (@eq-m09-cv) | $\text{CV} \propto \sqrt D$; $\text{CV}_L/\text{CV}_T = \sqrt{\sigma_{m,L}/\sigma_{m,T}}$ |
| Anisotropy (@eq-m09-anisotropy) | elliptical isochrones; $c(\theta)$ between $\text{CV}_T$ and $\text{CV}_L$ |
| Curvature (@eq-m09-curvature) | $c \approx c_0 - D\kappa$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Velocity ratio 3.0 and resistance ratios 3.6, 12.6, 9.4, 2.7 (calf trabeculae) | @clerc1976 |
| Velocity ratio 2.4, resistivity ratio 3.2 (canine epicardium) | @roberts1979 |
| 1.0 m/s normal-voltage, 0.6 m/s low-voltage left atrium | @heil2023 |
| Bidomain propagation 2% faster than monodomain | @potse2006 |
| Membrane constants | @nietoramos2023, based on @mitchell2003 |
| Velocities, grid errors, curvature fits, launch radii | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What is the length constant, and what sets it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The distance over which a held voltage decays to $1/e$ in a passive cable, $\sqrt{r_m/(r_i +
r_e)}$ (@eq-m09-cable).

</details>

**Q2. Write the bidomain equations in words.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Current leaving the intracellular space crosses the membrane as capacitive plus ionic current; total current
(intracellular plus extracellular) is conserved (@eq-m09-bidomain).

</details>

**Q3. When does the bidomain model reduce exactly to the monodomain model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In 1D, or when the extracellular conductivity tensor is a multiple of the intracellular one (equal anisotropy
ratios); then $\sigma_m = \sigma_i(\sigma_i + \sigma_e)^{-1}\sigma_e$ (@eq-m09-monodomain).

</details>

**Q4. When would you insist on a bidomain model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When current is applied, as in pacing-field or defibrillation studies. For propagation alone, organ-scale comparisons
found differences of about 2% [@potse2006].

</details>

**Q5. You double the conductivity. What happens to the velocity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It rises by $\sqrt 2$, about 41% (@eq-m09-cv).

</details>

**Q6. Velocity ratio along/across fibers is 3. What is the conductivity ratio?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

9, for the monodomain conductivity (@eq-m09-cv).

</details>

**Q7. Why are isochrones from a point elliptical?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Velocity is highest along fibers and lowest across them, so the far-field activation time is
$\sqrt{x_L^2/\text{CV}_L^2 + x_T^2/\text{CV}_T^2}$ (@eq-m09-anisotropy).

</details>

**Q8. A map reports 0.5 m/s along a line in tissue with 1.0 m/s along fibers and a ratio of 3. What else could explain it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The line may be oblique to the fibers: at about 40° the apparent speed is near 0.5 m/s (@eq-m09-anisotropy).
Curvature near the source and the method of estimation also matter.

</details>

**Q9. Why do waves slow near a small pacing electrode?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The front is strongly curved, so each bit of excited tissue must depolarize more tissue ahead of it:
$c \approx c_0 - D\kappa$ (@eq-m09-curvature) [@fast1997].

</details>

**Q10. What is a source–sink mismatch?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Too little depolarizing current to bring a larger region of resting tissue to threshold, as when a wave leaves a
narrow channel or a stimulus excites too small a region (@eq-m09-curvature) [@fast1997].

</details>

**Q11. Your simulated velocity changes when you halve the grid spacing. What does that mean?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The grid is too coarse for the front: refine until the velocity stops changing, or tune conductivity at the grid you
will use (@eq-m09-cv).

</details>

**Q12. Why might the extracellular potential matter even if the monodomain model is enough for propagation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Electrograms are extracellular signals. They can be computed from the monodomain solution with a separate
volume-conductor step (m02, m03).

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. $r_m$ = 4, $r_i + r_e$ = 1 (consistent units). Length constant?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

2 (@eq-m09-cable).

</details>

**S2. $\sigma_i$ = 1, $\sigma_e$ = 3 along a fiber. Monodomain conductivity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.75 (@eq-m09-monodomain).

</details>

**S3. Velocity 0.5 m/s at $D$; what at $4D$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1.0 m/s (@eq-m09-cv).

</details>

**S4. $\text{CV}_L$ = 1.0, $\text{CV}_T$ = 0.5 m/s. Apparent speed at 90° to the fibers?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.5 m/s (@eq-m09-anisotropy).

</details>

**S5. $c_0$ = 0.34 m/s, $D$ = 0.1 mm²/ms. Speed of a circular front of radius 5 mm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 0.34 − 0.02 = 0.32 m/s (@eq-m09-curvature).

</details>

**S6. Which model would you use to simulate a defibrillation shock?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The bidomain model (@eq-m09-bidomain).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Elliptical spread on the epicardium.** Roberts and colleagues show isochrones elongated along the fibers
  [@roberts1979]. This module: anisotropy.
- **Curvature and block.** Fast and Kléber illustrate fronts emerging from narrow structures and around obstacles
  [@fast1997]. This module: curvature.
- **Monodomain against bidomain.** Potse and colleagues compare activation and electrograms from both models
  [@potse2006]. This module: bidomain and monodomain.

## Further reading

- **Measurements.** Directional differences of impulse spread [@clerc1976; @roberts1979].
- **Theory and reviews.** Curvature [@fast1997]; mechanisms of propagation [@kleber2004]; monodomain against bidomain
  [@potse2006].
- **Mapping data.** Regional left atrial velocities [@heil2023].
- **Related modules.** m02 (volume conduction), m08 (action potentials), m10 (arrhythmia mechanisms), m25 (conduction
  velocity), m33 (digital twins), m42 (eikonal models).
